etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English me, from Old English mē (“me”, originally dative, but later also accusative), from Proto-West Germanic *miʀ, from Proto-Germanic *miz (“me”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁me- (“me”).

definitions.definition: As the object (direct or indirect) of a verb.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 86:17:
quote.text: Shew me a token foꝛ good, that they which hate me may ſee it, and bee aſhamed: becauſe thou, Lord, hast holpen me, and comfoꝛted me.

definitions.definition: (archaic, proscribed) Myself; as a reflexive direct object of a verb.

quote.citation: 1819, John Keats, La Belle Dame sans Merci:
quote.text: And I awoke, and found me here.

definitions.definition: (colloquial, proscribed) Myself; as a reflexive indirect object of a verb; the ethical dative.

quote.text: When I get to college, I'm gonna get me a white Nissan Sentra.

definitions.definition: As the object of a preposition.
The first-person singular, as the object (of a verb, preposition, etc).
(sometimes proscribed) As the complement of the copula (be).

quote.citation: 2017, Theresa May, “Andrew Neil interviews Theresa May: full transcript”, in The Spectator‎[1], archived from the original on 22 May 2017:
quote.text: It's either me or Jeremy Corbyn.

definitions.definition: Used for the pronoun in isolation or in apposition.
(informal, with a conjunction, often proscribed) As the subject of a verb.
(nonstandard, not with a conjunction) As the subject of a verb. Sometimes used to indicate or imitate limited English fluency.

quote.citation: 1844, Charles Wilkes, Narrative of the United States Exploring Expedition, volume II:
quote.text: One of them, whose sobriquet was Big-headed Blackboy, was stretched out before the fire, and no answer could be obtained from him, but a drawling repetition, in grunts of displeasure, of "Bel (not) me want to go.

quote.citation: 1899 July 20, Mrs. A[lexander] J[effrey] McKelway [i.e., Lavinia Rutherford McKelway], “Children’s Department”, in A[lexander] J[effrey] McKelway, editor, Presbyterian Standard, volume XLI, number 28, Charlotte, N.C.: The Presbyterian Publishing Company, page 14, column 1:
quote.text: Well he said me mustn’t eat ’nanas cause ’nanas would make me sick.

quote.citation: 2005 October 10, Michael Chapman; Matthew Chapman, “Teen Girl Squad Issue #10”, in Homestar Runner‎[2], spoken by Strong Bad (Matthew Chapman):
quote.text: Whoa! That was about the coolest thing ever! Me gotta see that again.

definitions.definition: (nonstandard, in apposition) Would be the subject of a copula in standard English, though the copula is omitted; used to indicate or imitate limited English fluency.

quote.citation: 1932 June, Katherine Albert, “Hey! Hey! Here Comes Johnny”, in James R. Quirk, editor, Photoplay, volume XLII, number 1, Chicago, Ill.: Photoplay Publishing Company, page 119, column 2:
quote.text: “I should stick to Tarzan,” he [Johnny Weissmuller] explains. “You see, I’m no actor. Well, I didn’t have to act in ‘Tarzan, the Ape Man’—just said, ‘Me Tarzan, you Jane.’ I'll never be able to act.”The words do not occur in the film itself, nor in the original book by Burroughs. Instead, Tarzan says “Tarzan” and “Jane” repeatedly.

quote.citation: 1954 February 3, Mrs. John F. Underhill, “The Last Leaf; Chapter Three: Bear Tracks”, in Lawrence Maxwell, editor, Junior Guide, volume 2, number 5, Washington, D.C., page 7, column 2:
quote.text: May opened the door, and a huge Indian walked into the room. “Me Bear Tracks,” he said. “Me hungry.”

definitions.definition: (nonstandard or proscribed) I, the first-person singular, as the subject.
The self or personality of the speaker, especially their authentic self.

quote.citation: 1871, George MacDonald, “[At the Back of the North Wind] Out in the Storm”, in Harry Thurston Peck, Frank R[ichard] Stockton, Julian Hawthorne, editors, Masterpieces of the World’s Literature, Ancient and Modern: The Great Authors of the World with Their Master Productions, volume XIV, New York, N.Y.: American Literary Society, published 1899, pages 7514–7515:
quote.text: “Quite easily. Here you are taking care of a poor little boy with one arm, and there you are sinking a ship with the other. It can’t be like you.” “Ah, but which is me? I can’t be two mes, you know.” “No. Nobody can be two mes.” “Well, which me is me?” “Now I must think. There looks to be two.” “Yes. That’s the very point—You can’t be knowing the thing you don’t know, can you?” “No.” “Which me do you know?” “The kindest, goodest, best me in the world,” answered Diamond, clinging to North Wind.  […]  “Do you know the other me as well?” “No. I can’t. I shouldn’t like to.” “There it is. You don’t know the other me. You are sure of one of them?” “Yes.” “And you are sure there can’t be two mes?” “Yes.” “Then the me you don’t know must be the same as the me you do know—else there would be two mes?” “Yes.” “Then the other me you don’t know must be as kind as the me you do know?”

quote.citation: 1948 January, Rog Phillips [pseudonym; Roger Phillip Graham], “Hate”, in Amazing Stories, volume 22, number 1, Chicago, Ill.: Ziff-Davis Publishing Company, page 69, column 2:
quote.text: The question seems unanswerable, because if those same atoms were to be collected as they leave my body as waste in the normal process of metabolism, and in a year when my body contained all new atoms, those old atoms which were me a year ago were reformed into an exact replica of me down to the last thought and cell, would there be two mes?

quote.citation: 1990, Bei Dao [pseudonym; Zhao Zhenkai], translated by Bonnie S. McDougall and Susette Ternent Cooke, Waves, New York, N.Y.: New Directions Publishing, →ISBN, page 158:
quote.text: “In these last few days I keep feeling that I’m changing, changing into something I don’t quite recognize myself.” / “You’ve become more like yourself.” / “Could there be two mes?” / “Perhaps more than two.” / “It gets worse and worse. So which me do you actually love ?” / “All of them.” / “You’re being slippery.” Her lips curled slyly. “In fact you only love the me in your mind’s eye, and that me doesn’t exist, right?” / “No, that’s the combination of all the yous.” / She laughed. “It’s just as complicated as a mathematical calculation, if you end up with the three-headed, six-armed me, could you stand that?”

definitions.definition: (UK regional, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, colloquial) Alternative form of my

quote.citation: a. 1918, Wilfred Owen, “The Letter”, in Douglas Kerr, editor, The Works of Wilfred Owen, page 54:
quote.text: There don't seem much to say just now. / (Yer what? Then don't, yer ruddy cow! / And give us back me cigarette!)

quote.citation: 1994, John Hodge, Shallow Grave, spoken by Alex Law (Ewan McGregor):

quote.text: Get off me cheese! Get off! Get off!
"What have I ever done to prove me worth, or where I could at least say as I'd made a difference?"

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From mi (“third note of a major scale”) +‎ -e (“flat”), from Glover's solmization, Italian mi in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin mīra in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.

definitions.definition: (music) The solfeggio syllable used to indicate the flat of the third note of a major scale.
